key.label: Watch for easing
key.text: New supply closes grid capacity shortfalls; gas-turbine lead times shorten; Texas connections resume and approvals rise.

calls.depends: New supply arrives around 2030: turbine expansion, the PJM Interconnection backstop auction and new 765 kilovolt lines in Texas. Near-term data point the other way, so the rating reverts to Severe if these signposts do not turn.

sps.name: Capacity auctions
sps.track: PJM Interconnection's main capacity auction: shortfall against the reliability requirement, procured against target reserve margin, new generation cleared, and clearing price against the cap.

sps.summary: Reserve margin 14.7% against a 20.0% target at the last auction
sps.latest: Shortfall 6,831 megawatts against the reliability requirement; total reserve margin 14.7% against a 20.0% target. 525 megawatts of new generation and uprates cleared. Price at the cap of $325 per megawatt-day; $555 simulated without the cap.

sps.name: Texas connections
sps.track: Whether Texas resumes approving large data centre connections: statements and measures from the incoming Governor and Legislature that would extend, widen or lift the pause; the audit of the queue; and, behind those, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) queue of large loads of 75 megawatts or more and the capacity approved to energise.
sps.trigger: Positive if approvals grow faster than about 2 gigawatts a year, the approved share rises and the queue stops growing.
sps.headline: Paused
sps.summary: Approvals on hold since 3 Aug 2026; the Governor-elect has pledged a moratorium
sps.latest: The Governor-elect has pledged a moratorium on data centre approvals until the Legislature passes new protections; she takes office on 19 Jan 2027 and can replace the current directives. Approvals to energise large data centres have been paused since 3 Aug 2026, and passing the audit does not by itself restart them. She repeated the call on 19 Nov 2026 and accepted that she cannot stop sites already under construction. A Senate bill filed for the session that opens on 12 Jan 2027, reported as Senate Bill 338 with 17 senators behind it, all but one of them Republican, would from 1 Sep 2027 limit new data centres to water-saving cooling, require yearly reports of water use and refuse a grid connection to sites that fall short. It is a filed bill, not law, and it neither extends nor lifts the current pause. Since 12 Nov, environmental permit reviews have resumed. The queue stood at about 475 gigawatts in June 2026, of which about 9 (roughly 2%) had approval.
sps.next: Audit report 10 Dec 2026; Legislature convenes 12 Jan 2027; new Governor 19 Jan 2027
sps.sources: ERCOT large-load status updates and monthly operational overview; Public Utility Commission of Texas filings
sps.verify: The linked update confirms the pause and the audit date. The Governor-elect's pledge, her powers, the resumed permit reviews and the queue figures come from a law-firm briefing and press reports, not from primary documents. The Governor-elect's remarks of 19 Nov and the Senate bill are from a press report (KCBD, 19 Nov 2026); the bill text has not been read.

history.brief: Texas Governor-elect repeated her call for a moratorium on new data centre permits; a Senate bill tying connection to water-saving cooling was reported filed

sps.threshold: Trigger: approvals grow over 2 gigawatts a year

sps.name: Turbine supply
sps.track: Whether large gas turbines (215 megawatts and above) for US utilities are getting easier to buy: orders against shipments (is the queue growing?) and the earliest delivery slot on sale (how long is the wait?), across GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Doosan Enerbility, with Siemens Energy noted. US orders by maker are context.
sps.trigger: Positive if large-turbine orders fall below shipments, so backlogs stop rising, and delivery slots before 2030 reappear.
sps.headline: Turbine waiting list still growing
sps.summary: Last quarter GE Vernova took orders for 11 gigawatts of turbines but delivered only 5, so its waiting list grew by 6. A turbine ordered today can't be delivered before 2029–30 (press-reported)
sps.latest: Is the queue growing? Yes. In the quarter to 30 Sep 2026 GE Vernova, the largest supplier to US utilities, signed 11 gigawatts of gas equipment and shipped 5, so orders ran 2.2 times shipments; its backlog plus slot reservations rose from 116 to 122 gigawatts. How long is the wait? Delivery slots at GE Vernova and Siemens Energy stretch into 2029 and 2030, according to press reports of their results. Who supplies the US? US orders for large gas turbines totalled 29 units in the first half of 2026: GE Vernova 13, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries 8, Doosan Enerbility 7 and Siemens Energy 1, according to McCoy Power Reports as cited in the press.
sps.next: Next quarterly results of GE Vernova and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries
sps.sources: US Securities and Exchange Commission filings (GE Vernova); Mitsubishi Heavy Industries quarterly results; Doosan Enerbility order announcements; Siemens Energy results; earnings-call reporting on delivery slots; industry order counts reported in the press (McCoy Power Reports, S&P Global)

key.label: Eases to Minor if
key.text: Zero-water, closed-loop cooling becomes the norm for new capacity; hub utilities expand reclaimed water; states fund water supply ahead of data centre demand; growth tilts to water-rich basins.

calls.depends: Water stays a cost and a siting filter, not a hard stop, as developers adapt instead of leaving. Waterless cooling uses more electricity, and most of a data centre's water footprint sits in power generation that operators do not control. It intensifies to Severe if Colorado River cuts deepen, states turn disclosure rules into hard limits, or drought leads utilities to refuse supply.
calls.bottom_line: Water holds at Moderate in both periods: it adds cost and steers where sites go, but developers adapt with closed-loop cooling and reclaimed water instead of leaving. The risks run both ways, to Minor or to Severe.

sps.name: Closed-loop becomes standard
sps.track: Whether zero-water, closed-loop designs become the norm for new US capacity, as shown in hyperscale operators' water disclosures and new state reporting (California, New Jersey, Utah).
sps.trigger: Positive if on-site water use stays well below the national laboratory's projection for 2028.
sps.headline: Microsoft: all new designs
sps.summary: Use zero-evaporation closed loops since August 2024. Not yet shown to be the norm across new US capacity
sps.latest: All new Microsoft data centre designs since August 2024 use zero-evaporation closed-loop cooling. Project Blue near Tucson moved away from evaporative cooling after the city blocked its original plan. The benchmark is Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's projection: US data centres used about 17 billion gallons directly in 2023, and hyperscale sites alone could use 16 to 33 billion gallons by 2028.
sps.next: Next round of operator water disclosures; first state water reports
sps.sources: Operators' sustainability reports; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; state water reporting in California, New Jersey and Utah
sps.verify: Baseline reading from the analysis behind this call (23 Nov 2026). The primary source has not yet been checked.

sps.track: Whether the share of new capacity going to water-stressed basins falls as growth tilts to water-rich regions such as the Great Lakes.

Microsoft expects its Great Lakes campuses to stay far below the Great Lakes Compact's regional-review trigger.

sps.name: Colorado River shortage
sps.track: Whether Lake Mead falls below 1,010 feet in the Bureau of Reclamation's monthly 24-Month Study projections, and how deep the next guidelines cut.
sps.trigger: Negative if Lake Mead is projected below 1,010 feet, which triggers consultation on deeper cuts, or if the next guidelines (from 2029) cut beyond 1.25 million acre-feet.
sps.headline: 1.25 million acre-feet cut
sps.summary: A year, in Lower Basin deliveries for 2027–28. Arizona loses 760,000 acre-feet, about 27% of its allocation
sps.latest: The Colorado River, which supplies the Phoenix, Tucson and Las Vegas hubs, is at record lows. Lower Basin deliveries are cut by 1.25 million acre-feet a year in 2027–28, with Arizona losing 760,000 acre-feet, about 27% of its allocation. Lake Mead could be projected below 1,010 feet by summer 2027. The framework allows cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet, with central Arizona first in line.
sps.next: Monthly 24-Month Study; possible breach by summer 2027
sps.sources: US Bureau of Reclamation 24-Month Study; US Department of the Interior
sps.verify: Baseline reading from the analysis behind this call (23 Nov 2026). The primary source has not yet been checked.
sps.threshold: Trigger: Lake Mead projected below 1,010 feet, or cuts beyond 1.25 million acre-feet

sps.name: Hard limits in law
sps.track: Whether 2027 state legislatures turn water disclosure rules into hard limits.
sps.trigger: Negative if a state enacts hard limits on data centre water use or pauses approvals, for example Texas Senate Bill 338 or a statewide pause in Arizona.
sps.headline: Disclosure, not limits
sps.summary: State rules so far mostly require reporting. Texas Senate Bill 338 and an Arizona pause are proposed, not law
sps.latest: Rules are tightening, so far mostly through disclosure. From 2027 California requires a water-supply assessment before approving a data centre and makes developers fund the water infrastructure they need. Virginia, New Jersey and Utah now require water reporting. Locally, Marana bars drinking water for data centre cooling and Chandler caps data centre water use. Proposed: Texas Senate Bill 338 (water-efficient cooling for new data centres), under a Governor-elect who has pledged to pause approvals, and a statewide pause backed by Arizona's new legislature and Attorney General.
sps.next: Texas Legislature convenes 12 Jan 2027; Arizona session opens Jan 2027
sps.sources: Texas Legislature Online; Arizona Legislature; state bill trackers
sps.verify: Baseline reading from the analysis behind this call (23 Nov 2026). The primary source has not yet been checked.

sps.name: Community benefit deals
sps.track: Number and value of host-community deals, and whether they turn opposition into approvals.
sps.trigger: Positive if deals convert opposed projects into approvals.
sps.headline: US$1 million per megawatt
sps.summary: New York's recommended local investment; one county's approvals with community payments are a first example to watch
sps.latest: New York published a voluntary framework on 15 Sep 2026 recommending at least US$1 million per megawatt in local investment. A first example to watch: on 16 Nov 2026 Spartanburg County, South Carolina, which has a moratorium in force and rejected a large project earlier in the year, gave final approval to three data centre agreements; the county puts community benefit payments at about US$60 million across five projects. It is not shown that the payments won the approvals: the developers also agreed to smaller sites and cleaner fuel. One county is not yet evidence of deals turning opposition into approvals at scale.
sps.next: Monthly check
sps.sources: New York Department of Public Service; Virginia Governor's office; Loudoun and Prince William board minutes
sps.verify: The New York framework is confirmed at the linked source. The Spartanburg County approvals are from a press report only (Fox Carolina, 18 Nov 2026); the county's own record has not been checked. Virginia's toolkit has not been checked.
sps.threshold: Trigger: deals turn opposition into approvals

calls.bottom_line: Land stays Severe in both periods: local opposition blocks or delays over half of large projects, and no state or federal override of local vetoes is in sight.

sps.name: Spain's final rules
sps.track: Whether the data centre decree is approved before the general election, and its final terms.
sps.trigger: Watch the 80% hourly renewables match, the 10 megawatt threshold and the five-year phase-in.
sps.headline: Approved
sps.summary: Spain's decree passed on 20 Nov 2026 with the 80% hourly renewables match kept; not yet in the official gazette, and a court challenge and the election lie ahead
sps.latest: Spain's Council of Ministers approved the royal decree on data centres on 20 Nov 2026, nine days before the general election. The terms this signpost watches all survived. Data centres must show that 80% of their electricity is matched hour by hour by renewable generation, most of it newly added to the grid. The grid-access rules apply to sites above 10 megawatts. For five years there is an easier route for sites that accept being disconnected first when the grid is short: 60% at peak hours until the end of 2028, then 70%. Sites that fall short can lose their grid-access rights for up to three years. Three things are not settled. The decree text had not appeared in the official gazette when this was written, so the date it takes effect is not known. The data centre industry association has said it will challenge the decree in court and ask for it to be suspended. The main opposition party, the Partido Popular (People's Party), has said it would repeal it, and the general election is on 29 Nov 2026. Why the opposition objects: its economy spokesman said the decree in practice prohibits new data centres and that the party would replace it with a law that allows them to be built. The regions it governs, among them Aragón and Madrid, host most of the large projects; Aragón's president said the decree makes many of the region's projects impossible and that he will challenge it. The government's case: the energy minister said data centres have already been granted about 15 gigawatts of grid access, roughly 40% of Spain's peak demand, and that without the decree households and businesses would pay about €5 billion more on their bills and industry about 25% more for energy.
sps.next: General election 29 Nov 2026; then publication in the official gazette and any court challenge
sps.sources: Spain's official gazette; Council of Ministers references; energy ministry; Council of State

sps.name: Spain's final rules on water
sps.track: Whether the final decree keeps the top water-efficiency class for new data centres above 10 megawatts.
sps.trigger: The draft requires 0.1 litres per kilowatt-hour or less.
sps.headline: Approved
sps.summary: Spain's decree passed on 20 Nov 2026 keeping the top water-efficiency level; which sites it covers and when it takes effect are not yet stated
sps.latest: Spain's Council of Ministers approved the royal decree on data centres on 20 Nov 2026, nine days before the general election. The water rule survived: data centres must meet the highest level for water use on the European Union's data centre label, which is still being drawn up. Until that label applies, the ceiling is 0.1, the figure in the draft (there, litres of water per kilowatt-hour). The ministry has not yet said which data centres the water rule covers (the draft applied it to new sites above 10 megawatts) or from when. Three things are not settled. The decree text had not appeared in the official gazette when this was written, so the date it takes effect is not known. The data centre industry association has said it will challenge the decree in court and ask for it to be suspended. The main opposition party, the Partido Popular (People's Party), has said it would repeal it, and the general election is on 29 Nov 2026. Why the opposition objects: its economy spokesman said the decree in practice prohibits new data centres, and the regions it governs, among them Aragón and Madrid, host most of the large projects. Its objections are aimed at the electricity rules; none found so far is aimed at the water rule, but a repeal would remove both. The government's case is that data centres' demand on the grid would otherwise raise bills for households and industry.
sps.next: General election 29 Nov 2026; then publication in the official gazette, which should show which sites the water rule covers
sps.sources: Spain's official gazette; energy ministry; river-basin authorities

history.note: Council of Ministers approved the royal decree on data centres, keeping the top water-efficiency level; status set to Turned negative by the owner on 21 Nov 2026

sps.name: Drought
sps.track: Share of the European Union and United Kingdom under drought warning or alert, especially Italy, Spain and Portugal.
sps.trigger: Wider or longer droughts confirm the intensification.

Hotspots were France, Germany, Hungary, Romania and the United Kingdom. In early November 2026 the European Drought Observatory said drought conditions remained critical in most of Europe and had worsened in the Iberian Peninsula; it gave no share of territory.
sps.next: Summer 2027 season

sps.track: Share of new European Union data centre capacity sited in basins under high water stress.

calls.bottom_line: Water rises from Minor to Moderate after 2030, as growth moves into the water-scarce south and rules start to make water use a condition for building.

key.label: Eases to Minor if
key.text: The European Union's fast-track permitting survives with a 12-month cap; England's national consent route is adopted and delivers; France's fast-track produces permits that survive court challenges.

calls.depends: Land decides where and how fast capacity is built, not whether it is. As power-short core hubs close, capacity moves to secondary, brownfield and peripheral sites, where fast-tracks shorten approvals but larger campuses draw more organised opposition. The two forces broadly offset, but fast-track routes are untested and contested. It intensifies to Severe if rejections keep rising, local bans spread, national decision-makers side against developers on appeal, or powered-land prices keep climbing.
calls.bottom_line: Land holds at Moderate in both periods: scarce, zoned land in the core hubs and rising local refusals are broadly offset by national fast-track routes. Those routes are untested, so the risks run both ways, to Minor or to Severe.

sps.name: EU fast-track permitting
sps.track: Whether the European Union's Cloud and AI Development Act keeps mandatory acceleration zones with a 12-month permit cap, and whether member states place zones where grid capacity is available.
sps.trigger: Positive if the act keeps mandatory acceleration zones and the 12-month cap.
sps.headline: 12-month cap proposed
sps.summary: The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act would cap permitting in acceleration zones at 12 months; unlikely to bite before about 2029
sps.latest: The European Union's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act would cap permitting in acceleration zones at 12 months. The Council takes up its compromise on the data centre part from 24 Nov 2026, and the European Parliament's position is planned for April 2027. The act is unlikely to bite before about 2029.
sps.next: Council talks from 24 Nov 2026; Parliament's position April 2027
sps.sources: Council of the European Union; European Parliament legislative observatory; European Commission
sps.verify: Baseline reading from the analysis behind this call (23 Nov 2026). The primary source has not yet been checked.
sps.threshold: Trigger: 12-month cap and mandatory zones survive

sps.name: UK national route
sps.track: Whether England adopts its data centre National Policy Statement with the proposed presumption of consent and 100 megawatt threshold intact, and whether the projects already in the national regime are consented within about 18 months.
sps.trigger: Positive if the statement is adopted intact and the three directed projects, such as Wapseys Wood, are consented within about 18 months.
sps.headline: Consultation open
sps.summary: England's draft National Policy Statement proposes a presumption of consent above 100 megawatts; consultation closes 8 Jan 2027
sps.latest: England offers an opt-in national consent route alongside five AI Growth Zones. Its draft data centre National Policy Statement proposes a presumption of consent and a 100 megawatt threshold; the consultation closes on 8 Jan 2027. Three projects, including Wapseys Wood, were directed into the national regime by July 2026.
sps.next: Consultation closes 8 Jan 2027
sps.sources: UK government consultations; Planning Inspectorate national infrastructure register
sps.verify: Baseline reading from the analysis behind this call (23 Nov 2026). The primary source has not yet been checked.

sps.name: France's fast-track
sps.track: Whether France grants major-national-interest status to large data centres, how many of its 63 ready sites win permits, and whether those permits survive court challenges.
sps.trigger: Positive if France grants the status, permits follow, and they survive in court.
sps.headline: None granted yet
sps.summary: No large data centre had major-national-interest status by mid-October 2026. 63 ready sites identified, 26 already secured
sps.latest: France can designate data centres as projects of major national interest and has identified 63 data-centre-ready sites, 26 of them already secured. No large data centre had been granted the status by mid-October 2026. In July 2026 a French court suspended the permit for a 40 megawatt AI data centre at Alixan.
sps.next: Monthly check of decrees and court rulings

sps.name: Projects rejected or restricted

sps.trigger: Negative if the count keeps rising after 2026.
sps.headline: Over 70 in four months
sps.summary: Projects rejected or restricted in January to April 2026, more than in all of 2025
sps.latest: More than 70 projects were rejected or restricted in January to April 2026, more than in all of 2025, according to the European Data Centre Monitor. Councils from Groß-Gerau near Frankfurt to Cologno Monzese near Milan and Pyhäjoki in Finland have refused schemes.
sps.next: Next update of the European Data Centre Monitor

sps.name: Local bans spread
sps.track: Whether zoning bans and pauses spread beyond the Netherlands and Scotland, and whether Scotland's guidance reopens consents on clear terms.
sps.trigger: Negative if bans or pauses spread to further countries or hubs. Scotland reopening consents on clear terms would count the other way.
sps.headline: Netherlands and Scotland
sps.summary: Dutch zoning confines hyperscale sites to two areas; Scotland has paused hyperscale decisions pending national guidance
sps.latest: The Netherlands confines new hyperscale data centres (over 10 hectares and 70 megawatts) to two designated areas, and Amsterdam and Zaanstad bar new data centres above 2,000 square metres and 5 megavolt-amperes. Frankfurt limits new colocation data centres to designated districts. Scotland has paused hyperscale decisions pending national guidance: a progress report is due by end-2026 and full guidance by September 2027.
sps.next: Scotland's progress report by end-2026; full guidance by Sep 2027
sps.sources: Scottish Government planning guidance; Dutch national and municipal zoning rules; city of Frankfurt
sps.verify: Baseline reading from the analysis behind this call (23 Nov 2026). The primary source has not yet been checked.
sps.threshold: Trigger: bans or pauses spread beyond the Netherlands and Scotland

calls.bottom_line: Power eases from Severe to Moderate after 2030 if Korea and Japan succeed in routing data centres to regions with spare grid, with nuclear restarts adding firm supply for Tokyo.

key.label: Stays contained if
key.text: Water supply keeps pace with data centre growth; data centres avoid water-stressed areas; operators shift away from water cooling.

calls.depends: Growth is concentrated in water-stressed hubs: Johor, Mumbai, Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor and West Java. In droughts, governments put households first.

sps.name: Supply and rules keep pace
sps.track: Johor's treated-water reserve margin against its pipeline of about 8.5 gigawatts; Thailand's siting standards; whether India's hubs avoid commercial water cuts in the 2027 dry season.
sps.trigger: Positive if supply and rules keep up with the pipeline.
sps.summary: Johor's reserve margin, statewide; a brokerage estimate says 12.8%
sps.latest: Johor reserve margin about 14.4% statewide, as stated in Parliament on 24 Jun 2026. A brokerage estimate puts it at about 12.8%.
sps.next: Thailand's board considers an 80% water-reuse rule on 27 Nov 2026
sps.sources: Malaysia's water regulator fact book; Ranhill SAJ filings; Thai reservoir data; Mumbai lake levels; India's reservoir bulletin
sps.verify: From press reports of the parliamentary statement (The Star). Thailand and India have not been checked.
sps.threshold: Trigger: supply and rules keep up with the pipeline

sps.name: Shift away from water cooling
sps.track: Share of new capacity using air-cooled or closed-loop systems; what Johor approves after its freeze; whether Thailand bars water-cooled sites from stressed areas.
sps.trigger: Positive if new approvals move to designs that use little water.
sps.headline: Air cooling only
sps.summary: Johor's stated approval policy; water-cooled expansions held to mid-2027
sps.latest: Johor's chief minister said on 10 Mar 2026 that the state's data centre committee will only approve Tier 3 and Tier 4 developments that use air cooling, and will refuse projects needing a high water intake. Johor is also reported to have asked operators to hold water-cooled expansions until mid-2027.
sps.next: Freeze ends mid-2027 at the earliest
sps.sources: Johor state government; Malaysian Investment Development Authority; Thailand Board of Investment; Uptime Institute survey

history.note: Johor's chief minister: only air-cooled Tier 3 and Tier 4 data centres will be approved

sps.verify: The air-cooling statement is confirmed at the linked Bernama interview. It is a stated policy; what has actually been approved since is not verified. The hold on water-cooled expansions until mid-2027 is from press reports only.
sps.threshold: Trigger: approvals move to low-water designs

calls.bottom_line: Water rises from Moderate to Severe after 2030: growth is concentrated in water-stressed hubs, and in droughts governments put households first.

insight: To 2030, power is the binding constraint in North America, Europe and North Asia. After 2030 it eases in North America and North Asia, but Europe's core hubs wait for grid fixes into the 2030s, and growth moving into water-stressed areas makes water the rising constraint in southern Europe and South and Southeast Asia.
coverage_note: The tracker follows eight region and constraint pairs: the four where the rating changes between 2026–30 and beyond 2030, the two where a Severe rating persists, and the two Moderate pairs that complete the picture for North America and Europe, where the question is whether Moderate eases to Minor or intensifies to Severe.
